Pinch’s conjecture on aa-convexity

John M. Campbell Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS B3H 4R2, Canada Email address: jh241966@dal.ca
Abstract.

For aa in ℝ\mathbb{R}, a subset VV contained in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is said to be aa-convex if x,y∈V⟹a​x+(1−a)​y∈V\text{{\bf x}},\text{{\bf y}}\in V\Longrightarrow a\text{{\bf x}}+(1-a)\text{{\bf y}}\in V. According to Pinch [Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc., 1985], the aa-convex hull of VV is the intersection of all of the aa-convex subsets of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} that contain VV, and Pinch also defines D⁡(a)D(a) as the aa-convex hull of {0,1}\{0,1\} in ℝ1\mathbb{R}^{1}. Pinch conjectured that if aa is a totally real algebraic integer and D⁡(a)D(a) has no limit points, then every algebraic conjugate of aa other than aa is in (0,1)(0,1). We succeed in proving this conjecture, which seems to have remained open.

Key words and phrases: 
convex hull, algebraic integer, totally real number, algebraic conjugate, Bernstein basis polynomial
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11R04; Secondary 41A10

1. Introduction

The purpose of this paper is to prove a conjecture due to Pinch [6] related to what Pinch refers to as an aa-convex set, referring to the preliminaries covered below. Based on extant work citing Pinch’s paper [1, 2, 4, 5, 7], it appears that Pinch’s conjecture has remained open. Our proof of Pinch’s conjecture is based on our extensive interactions with GPT-5.6 Pro.

Recall that an algebraic integer is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in ℤ\mathbb{Z}. For an algebraic number α\alpha, letting mα​(X)∈ℚ​[X]m_{\alpha}(X)\in\mathbb{Q}[X] denote its minimal polynomial over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, an algebraic conjugate of α\alpha refers to any complex root of mα​(X)m_{\alpha}(X). An algebraic number is said to be totally real if each algebraic conjugate of this number is a real number. A nontrivial conjugate of α\alpha refers to a conjugate distinct from α\alpha.

Following Pinch’s work [6], a set V⊆ℝnV\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is aa-convex for a value a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} if: For all x and y in VV, we have that a​x+(1−a)​ya\text{{\bf x}}+(1-a)\text{{\bf y}} is in VV. Also, the aa-convex hull of VV is defined by Pinch as the intersection of the aa-convex subsets that contain VV and that are contained in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Pinch also defines D⁡(a)D(a) as the aa-convex hull of {0,1}\{0,1\} in ℝ\mathbb{R}.

For an indeterminate XX, let D0​(X)={0,1}D_{0}(X)=\{0,1\}. We then recursively define Dn+1​(X)D_{n+1}(X) so that Dn+1(X)={Xf(X)+(1−X)g(X):f,g∈Dn(X)}D_{n+1}(X)=\{Xf(X)+(1-X)g(X):f,g\in D_{n}(X)\}. Moreover, we let D⁡(X)=⋃n=0∞Dn​(X)D(X)=\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}D_{n}(X), and for a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}, we let

(1) D⁡(a)={f⁡(a):f∈D⁡(X)}.D(a)=\{f(a):f\in D(X)\}.

It is proved by Pinch [6, Proposition 1] that D⁡(a)D(a), as defined in (1), is the aa-convex hull of {0,1}\{0,1\}. Again adopting notation from Pinch, a real parameter aa is said to be sparse if D⁡(a)D(a) does not have any limit points.

Pinch [6, Proposition 12] proved that: If a∉(0,1)a\not\in(0,1) is a totally real algebraic integer and if each nontrivial conjugate of aa is in (0,1)(0,1), then aa is sparse. Pinch also proved the converse for the quadratic case, and considered the problem as to whether or not the converse holds in full generality. This is made explicit below, via what we refer to as Pinch’s conjecture, as given in an equivalent way by Pinch in 1985.

Pinch’s conjecture: Let aa denote a totally real algebraic integer. If aa is sparse, then each conjugate of aa distinct from aa is in (0,1)(0,1).

The main purpose of this paper is to prove Pinch’s conjecture, as in Section 2 below.

2. Main result

The following result is required for our purposes and was established by Pinch [6, Corollary 4.1], and we thus omit a proof of the following result from Pinch.

Lemma 1.

(Pinch, 1985) For each n≥0n\geq 0, the equality

Dn(X)={∑k=0nckXk(1−X)n−k:ck∈ℤ, 0≤ck≤(nk)}D_{n}(X)=\left\{\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_{k}X^{k}(1-X)^{n-k}:c_{k}\in\mathbb{Z},\ 0\leq c_{k}\leq\binom{n}{k}\right\}

holds [6, Corollary 4.1].

For 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n, we let Bernstein basis polynomials be defined and denoted so that

(2) Bk,n​(X)=(nk)​Xk​(1−X)n−k.B_{k,n}(X)=\binom{n}{k}X^{k}(1-X)^{n-k}.

For fixed nn, the family of expressions of the form shown in (2) is a basis of {p⁡(X)∈ℝ⁡[X]:deg⁡p≤n}\{p(X)\in\mathbb{R}[X]:\deg p\leq n\}.

Lemma 2.

Let R∈ℝ⁡[X]R\in\mathbb{R}[X] satisfy R⁡(x)>0R(x)>0 for x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1) and R⁡(0),R⁡(1)≥0R(0),R(1)\geq 0. Then, for all sufficiently large nn, the coefficients of RR as a linear combination of expressions of the form Bk,n​(X)B_{k,n}(X) are all nonnegative.

Proof.

We begin with the factorization

(3) R⁡(X)=Xr​(1−X)s​H​(X)R(X)=X^{r}(1-X)^{s}H(X)

for r,s≥0r,s\geq 0 and where neither 1−X1-X nor XX divides H⁡(X)H(X), noting that R⁡(X)R(X) is not the zero polynomial from the assumption that R⁡(x)>0R(x)>0 for x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1). From the assumption that RR is positive on (0,1)(0,1), this and (3) together give us that H⁡(x)>0H(x)>0 for x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1). The specified values of rr and ss are, respectively, the exact multiplicities of the zeros of RR at 00 and 11. This gives us that H⁡(0)≠0H(0)\neq 0 and that H⁡(1)≠0H(1)\neq 0. Since xrx^{r} and (1−x)s(1-x)^{s} are strictly positive for x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), and since H⁡(x)=R⁡(x)xr​(1−x)sH(x)=\frac{R(x)}{x^{r}(1-x)^{s}} is continuous and since R⁡(x)>0R(x)>0 for x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), we find that H⁡(0)=limx→0+H⁡(x)≥0H(0)=\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}H(x)\geq 0. From this and H⁡(0)≠0H(0)\neq 0 together, we have that H⁡(0)>0H(0)>0, and a symmetric argument allows us to similarly conclude that H⁡(1)>0H(1)>0. So, we have that H⁡(x)>0H(x)>0 for x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1]. Now, write

for real coefficients hjh_{j} for j∈{0,1,…,deg⁡H}j\in\{0,1,\ldots,\deg H\}. For an arbitrary integer m≥deg⁡Hm\geq\deg H, we obtain a unique degree-mm Bernstein expansion of H⁡(X)H(X), writing

with

From (3) and (5) together, we find that

The following Lemma is essentially the converse direction of Theorem 3.6 from the work of Fenner et al. [2].

Lemma 3.

Let P∈ℤ⁡[X]P\in\mathbb{Z}[X] be such that P⁡(0),P⁡(1)∈{0,1}P(0),P(1)\in\{0,1\} and such that P⁡(x)∈(0,1)P(x)\in(0,1) for each xx in (0,1)(0,1). Then PP is in D⁡(X)D(X) (cf. [2, Theorem 3.6]).

Proof.

Both PP and 1−P1-P satisfy the conditions of Lemma 2. Choose an integer N≥deg⁡PN\geq\deg P sufficiently large so that the conclusion of Lemma 2 holds, at degree NN, for both PP and 1−P1-P. We may then write

(13) P⁡(X)=∑k=0Nβk,N​Bk,N​(X),P(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\beta_{k,N}B_{k,N}(X),

with βk,N≥0\beta_{k,N}\geq 0 for each coefficient of the form βk,N\beta_{k,N} arising in the expansion in (13). Since 1=∑k=0NBk,N​(X)1=\sum_{k=0}^{N}B_{k,N}(X) (recalling (2)), the coefficients of 1−P1-P arising as a linear combination of expressions of the form Bk,N​(X)B_{k,N}(X) are of the form 1−βk,N1-\beta_{k,N}. By our choice of NN, the Bernstein coefficients 1−βk,N1-\beta_{k,N} of 1−P1-P are nonnegative, and hence

(14) 0≤βk,N≤10\leq\beta_{k,N}\leq 1

for k∈{0,1,…,N}k\in\{0,1,\ldots,N\}.

Write P⁡(X)=∑j=0deg⁡Paj​XjP(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{\deg P}a_{j}X^{j}, where aj∈ℤa_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}. The binomial theorem gives us that Xj=∑k=jN(N−jk−j)​Xk​(1−X)N−kX^{j}=\sum_{k=j}^{N}\binom{N-j}{k-j}X^{k}(1-X)^{N-k} for all j∈{0,1,…,deg⁡P}j\in\{0,1,\ldots,\deg P\}. This allows us to rewrite P⁡(X)P(X) so that

(15) P⁡(X)=∑k=0Nck,N​Xk​(1−X)N−kP(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}c_{k,N}X^{k}(1-X)^{N-k}

for ck,N=∑j=0min⁡{k,deg⁡P}aj​(N−jk−j)c_{k,N}=\sum_{j=0}^{\min\{k,\deg P\}}a_{j}\binom{N-j}{k-j}, noting that the coefficients of the form ck,Nc_{k,N} are all integers. Comparing the coefficients in the expansions in (13) and (15) allows us to conclude that ck,N=(Nk)​βk,Nc_{k,N}=\binom{N}{k}\beta_{k,N}. From (14), we may deduce that 0≤ck,N≤(Nk)0\leq c_{k,N}\leq\binom{N}{k}, and Pinch’s lemma, as given as Lemma 1, allows us to conclude that P⁡(X)∈DN​(X)⊆D⁡(X)P(X)\in D_{N}(X)\subseteq D(X). ∎

The following result required for our purposes is a special case of a result due to Pinch [6, Proposition 10].

(Pinch, 1985) For a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}, if there exists an element PP in D⁡(X)D(X) such that 0<P⁡(a)<10<P(a)<1, then aa is not sparse [6, Proposition 10].

(16) J⁡(K,ℤ)={x∈K:p⁡(x)=0​for each​p∈B⁡(K,ℤ)}.J(K,\mathbb{Z})=\{x\in K:p(x)=0\ \text{for each}\ p\in B(K,\mathbb{Z})\}.

Lemma 6.

Let K⊆ℝK\subseteq\mathbb{R} be compact, with 0,1∈K0,1\in K. Assume that d⁡(K)<1d(K)<1 and J0​(K,ℤ)={0,1}J_{0}(K,\mathbb{Z})=\{0,1\}. Then there is a polynomial Q∈ℤ⁡[X]Q\in\mathbb{Z}[X] satisfying Q⁡(0)=Q⁡(1)=0Q(0)=Q(1)=0 and satisfying

(28) Q⁡(x)∈(0,1)Q(x)\in(0,1)

for each element xx in K∖{0,1}K\setminus\{0,1\}.

Proof.

From the assumptions such that K⊆ℝK\subseteq\mathbb{R} is compact, that d⁡(K)<1d(K)<1, and that J0​(K,ℤ)={0,1}J_{0}(K,\mathbb{Z})=\{0,1\}, the above formulation of Ferguson’s theorem [3, Theorem 6.4], as in Theorem 1 above, gives us that

Recalling that pp is a single-variable and nonzero polynomial, we find that pp has only finitely many real zeroes. This gives us that the right-hand side of (30) is finite, and we proceed to write 𝒵={x1,x2,…,xm}\mathcal{Z}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m}\}, allowing for the possibility that m=0m=0.

Again recalling (16), we find that xi∉J⁡(K,ℤ)x_{i}\not\in J(K,\mathbb{Z}) for each index ii ∈\in {1\{1, 22, …\ldots, m}m\}. Consequently, for each ii in {1,2,…,m}\{1,2,\ldots,m\}, there exists a polynomial pi∈B⁡(K,ℤ)p_{i}\in B(K,\mathbb{Z}) satisfying

(31) pi​(xi)≠0.p_{i}(x_{i})\neq 0.

Now, let x∈K∖{0,1}x\in K\setminus\{0,1\}. If p⁡(x)≠0p(x)\neq 0, then xx is not a common zero of the polynomials pp, p1p_{1}, p2p_{2}, …\ldots, pmp_{m}. 2.1. Proof of Pinch’s conjecture

Theorem 2.

Let aa denote a totally real algebraic integer. If aa is sparse, then each algebraic conjugate of aa distinct from aa is in (0,1)(0,1).

Proof.

Assume that aa is a sparse and totally real algebraic integer.

If aa is an integer, then the minimal polynomial (with respect to an indeterminate XX) of aa over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is X−aX-a, so that aa does not have any nontrivial algebraic conjugates, and the desired conclusion holds vacuously. So, we henceforth assume that aa is not an integer.

By way of contradiction, suppose that a∈(0,1)a\in(0,1). In this case, the identity polynomial P⁡(X)=XP(X)=X would be such that 0<P⁡(a)=a<10<P(a)=a<1, but then Pinch’s lemma, as formulated above in Lemma 4, would give us that aa would not be sparse, contradicting our above assumption that aa is sparse. So, we henceforth let aa be outside of (0,1)(0,1). Moreover, since we are letting aa be a non-integer, we have that

(39) a∉[0,1].a\not\in[0,1].

Now, by way of contradiction, assume that aa has a nontrivial conjugate a∗a^{\ast} such that

(40) a∗∉(0,1).a^{\ast}\not\in(0,1).

From the assumption that aa is totally real, we find that a∗∈ℝa^{\ast}\in\mathbb{R}. We see that a∗a^{\ast} could not be equal to 00, because, otherwise, letting ma​(X)m_{a}(X) denote the minimal polynomial of aa, we would have that ma​(0)=0m_{a}(0)=0, with XX dividing ma​(X)m_{a}(X), but the irreducibility of mam_{a} over ℚ\mathbb{Q} would thus imply that ma​(X)=Xm_{a}(X)=X, i.e., so that a=0a=0, but this contradicts (39) (and contradicts that a∉ℤa\not\in\mathbb{Z}). A symmetric argument gives us that a∗≠1a^{\ast}\neq 1, i.e., since, otherwise, we would have that ma​(X)=X−1m_{a}(X)=X-1, with a=1a=1. So, from (40), we obtain that

(41) a∗∉[0,1].a^{\ast}\not\in[0,1].

We proceed to define K=[0,1]∪{a}K=[0,1]\cup\{a\}. From (39), we find that Lemma 5 gives us that

(42) d⁡(K)<1,d(K)<1,

noting that a stronger estimate may be obtained from the proof of Lemma 5.

We see that

(43) {0,1}⊆J0​(K,ℤ),\{0,1\}\subseteq J_{0}(K,\mathbb{Z}),

since the conjugacy classes for 00 and 11 are {0}\{0\} and {1}\{1\}, respectively, and each of these singleton sets is contained in KK.

Now, let α∈J0​(K,ℤ)\alpha\in J_{0}(K,\mathbb{Z}). We thus have that the conjugacy class of α\alpha is contained in KK.

By way of contradiction, suppose that aa is a conjugate of α\alpha. So the minimal polynomial mα​(X)m_{\alpha}(X) would have aa as a root. Consequently, the minimal polynomial ma​(X)m_{a}(X) would divide mα​(X)m_{\alpha}(X) in ℚ⁡[X]\mathbb{Q}[X], and, since both of these polynomials are monic and irreducible, we would have that mα​(X)=ma​(X)m_{\alpha}(X)=m_{a}(X). So, the conjugacy classes of α\alpha and aa would be equal, i.e., so that the conjugacy class of α\alpha would necessarily contain a∗a^{\ast}, recalling that a∗a^{\ast} is defined as a nontrivial conjugate of aa. By definition of a nontrivial conjugate, we have that a∗≠aa^{\ast}\neq a, and this and (41) together give us that a∗∉K=[0,1]∪{a}a^{\ast}\not\in K=[0,1]\cup\{a\}. We thus obtain a contradiction, since the conjugacy class of α\alpha is contained in KK.

So, none of the conjugates of α\alpha equal aa. Since all of these conjugates are in K=[0,1]∪{a}K=[0,1]\cup\{a\}, all of the conjugates of α\alpha are in [0,1][0,1].

Let the conjugates of α\alpha be denoted with β1\beta_{1}, β2\beta_{2}, …\ldots, βd\beta_{d} for some positive integer dd. The preceding argument gives us that

(44) 0≤βi≤10\leq\beta_{i}\leq 1

for each index ii in {1,2,…,d}\{1,2,\ldots,d\}. If at least one expression of the form βi\beta_{i} were to be equal to 00, then the minimal polynomial mα​(X)m_{\alpha}(X) would be the identity polynomial, with mα​(X)=Xm_{\alpha}(X)=X, and this would give us that α=0\alpha=0. Alternatively, suppose that each expression of the form βi\beta_{i} were positive. The bounds in (44) would give us that

(45) 0<∏i=1dβi≤1.0<\prod_{i=1}^{d}\beta_{i}\leq 1.

From the assumption that α\alpha is an algebraic integer, we have that its minimal polynomial is monic and has coefficients in ℤ\mathbb{Z}, so that

(46) ∏i=1dβi=(−1)d​mα​(0)∈ℤ.\prod_{i=1}^{d}\beta_{i}=(-1)^{d}m_{\alpha}(0)\in\mathbb{Z}.

Since the left-hand side of the equality (46) is positive, i.e., from (45), the upper bound in (45), together with the left-hand side of the equation in (46) being an integer, gives us that ∏i=1dβi=1\prod_{i=1}^{d}\beta_{i}=1. Each expression of the form βi\beta_{i} is in (0,1](0,1], from (44) and (45) together. We see that a finite product of values in (0,1](0,1] equals 11 only when each factor equals 11, i.e., so that β1=β2=⋯=βd=1\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\cdots=\beta_{d}=1, which implies that α=1\alpha=1. This establishes the reverse inclusion corresponding to (43), writing

(47) J0​(K,ℤ)={0,1}.J_{0}(K,\mathbb{Z})=\{0,1\}.

So, from (42) and (47) together, we find that all of the conditions given in Lemma 6 hold. So, Lemma 6 gives us that there is a polynomial Q⁡(X)Q(X) in ℤ⁡[X]\mathbb{Z}[X] satisfying Q⁡(0)=Q⁡(1)=0Q(0)=Q(1)=0 and satisfying

(48) ∀x∈K∖{0,1}​ 0<Q⁡(x)<1.\forall x\in K\setminus\{0,1\}\ 0<Q(x)<1.

Noting the containment of (0,1)(0,1) in K∖{0,1}K\setminus\{0,1\}, we deduce that Q⁡(x)∈(0,1)Q(x)\in(0,1) for each member xx in (0,1)(0,1). From Lemma 3, we thus have that

(49) Q∈D⁡(X).Q\in D(X).

Moreover, since a∈K∖{0,1}a\in K\setminus\{0,1\} (recalling that K=[0,1]∪{a}K=[0,1]\cup\{a\} and recalling (39)), we find that (48) gives us that 0<Q⁡(a)<10<Q(a)<1. From this and (49) together, we find that Pinch’s lemma, as in Lemma 4 above, gives us that aa is not sparse, contradicting our initial assumption that aa is sparse. We have thus arrived at a contradiction giving us that it is not the case that aa has a nontrivial conjugate a∗a^{\ast} satisfying a∗∉(0,1)a^{\ast}\not\in(0,1). ∎
